title: x86-64 Assembly and Encoding
description: The three-byte VEX form is not for 256-bit registers, which it can name perfectly well; a register-to-register copy that the three-operand form eliminates was free; a failing cmov still reads its source, proved with a PROT_NONE page and not with a stopwatch; and the 0F 3A map is empty to two instructions in 256 and half full with one VEX byte in front.
author: Underlayer
completion_criteria: Read all 5 concepts, reproduce the 155 checks in courses/x86asm/assets/samples/crosscheck.py, then break the decoder's length arithmetic on purpose and make the group that catches it fail by name

modules.title: The Surface: What the Instructions Are
The Encoding: What the Bytes Are

concepts.title: Reading a Disassembly Without Being Fooled
concepts.description: Two syntaxes, one instruction, and the operand order that reverses between them: `addps %xmm1, %xmm0` and `addps xmm0, xmm1` are the same three bytes, and every tutorial that mixes them is describing two different instructions.

concepts.title: The Integer Set, Which Nothing Teaches
concepts.description: ADD and SUB chain at 3.65x and 3.25x; CMP and TEST, which all write the same one-bit-wide register, chain at 0.86x and 0.78x -- because the flags are renamed, which the ISA does not say and which no user-mode program can observe.

concepts.title: From a Comparison to a Boolean
concepts.description: A cmov whose condition FAILS still reads its source and still writes its destination, and a branch that fails touches neither -- proved with a PROT_NONE page, because the register results are identical and no stopwatch could ever have told you.

concepts.title: Two Bytes, Three, and the Bit That Went Wrong
concepts.description: The 0F 3A map is named in 2 of its 256 slots with the legacy escape and 54 of them with a three-byte VEX in front of the same slots, which is what the mmmmm field is for and the exact opposite of what this course was drafted to say about it.

concepts.title: The Audit, and the Reader That Agreed With Itself
concepts.description: Fifty-one corpus entries, two independent decoders, zero disagreements -- and a control that decodes the same bytes twice, agrees 100%, and is then poisoned and agrees 100% again, which is the cheapest demonstration in this collection of why a check that reads its own input twice proves nothing.
